name: PhishGuard scam-message rules
description: Educational rule base that turns warning signs in an email or text message into an explained scam assessment.

questions.text: Claims to be from a known company or bank
Sender's address does not belong to the company it names
A company is writing from a free email account (Gmail, Outlook…)
Replies would go to a different domain than the sender
Generic greeting such as "Dear customer"
Contains web links
Uses a link shortener that hides the real address
Names a company but links to a website that is not theirs
Link points to a raw IP address
Link text shows one address but points to another
Link or sender uses a lookalike of a real brand's domain
Link uses a domain ending often abused by scammers (.xyz, .top…)
Link uses plain http:// instead of https://
Pushes you to act immediately or within hours
Threatens suspension, locking, fines or legal action
Promises a prize, refund or reward
Asks you to keep it confidential or not tell anyone
Asks you to log in, verify an account or share a password or code
Asks you to send back a verification code you received
Asks for a payment, fee, gift cards or crypto
Asks for personal or card details
Mentions a risky attachment (.zip, .exe, .html, .iso…)

labels.impersonation: Pretends to be a trusted organisation
labels.hidden_destination: Hides where a link really goes
labels.credential_phishing: Credential phishing (tries to steal your login)

dont_enter_credentials.title: Don't log in through this message
dont_enter_credentials.advice: Do not click the link or enter any password or code. If you already did, change that password now and turn on two-factor authentication.

dont_pay.title: Don't send money
dont_pay.advice: Do not pay, buy gift cards or send crypto. Genuine organisations do not ask for payment this way.

dont_open_attachment.title: Don't open the attachment
dont_open_attachment.advice: Do not open or download the attachment. If you did, disconnect from the internet and run a security scan.

protect_identity.title: Keep your details private
protect_identity.advice: Do not send card numbers, ID documents or personal details in reply to this message.

verify_independently.title: Verify through an official channel
verify_independently.advice: Contact the company using the app, website or phone number you already know, not the details in this message.

check_link_destination.title: Inspect the link first
check_link_destination.advice: Hover over (or long-press) the link to see its real address before doing anything. Type the official address yourself instead.

confirm_with_sender.title: Confirm in person
confirm_with_sender.advice: Check the request with the person directly, by phone or face to face, before acting on it.

slow_down.title: Take your time
slow_down.advice: Scammers rely on urgency. A genuine deadline will survive a few minutes of checking.

report_message.title: Report and delete
report_message.advice: Report the message as phishing in your email app (or forward scam texts to your carrier's spam number), then delete it.

never_share_codes.title: Never share a code
never_share_codes.advice: Never forward a verification code to anyone, even a friend. Whoever has the code can take over your account. If you already sent it, secure the account and log out other devices.

rules.because: The address does not match the organisation it claims to be.
Replies are routed somewhere other than the apparent sender.
A brand name combined with a forged-looking sender is classic impersonation.
Lookalike domains exist to borrow a real brand's trust.
Real companies do not send official notices from free webmail accounts.
A company that knows you would normally use your name.
The message uses a company's name but sends you to someone else's website.
Shorteners hide the real destination of a link.
The visible address and the real target differ.
Legitimate services use domain names, not bare IP addresses.
A link that hides its destination should not be trusted.
The link leads to a domain imitating a real brand.
This domain ending is cheap and frequently used for throwaway scam sites.
Asking for a login over an unencrypted link is a red flag.
Urgency plus a threat is designed to stop you thinking.
Artificial deadlines push people to act before checking.
Fear of losing access is a common manipulation.
Unexpected rewards are bait to get you to engage.
Asking for secrecy stops you from checking with others.
An impersonator asking you to log in is trying to capture your credentials.

Pressure to pay quickly is how payment scams work.
An impersonator asking for money is a payment scam.
Paying a fee to receive a prize is the advance-fee scam pattern.

A disguised sender plus a risky attachment is a typical malware campaign.
A code request under time pressure is a typical takeover attempt.
